sources.ref_file_title: FO99 - Secure Integration of Asymmetric and Symmetric Encryption Schemes
sources.note: Introduces the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform: generic conversion of a weakly (one-way / IND-CPA) secure asymmetric scheme into an IND-CCA-secure hybrid scheme in the ROM. Journal version: J. Cryptology 26(1), 2013, doi:10.1007/s00145-011-9114-1.

sources.ref_file_title: HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation
sources.authors: Dennis Hofheinz, Kathrin Hövelmanns, Eike Kiltz
sources.note: Decomposes FO into the T and U transforms, states the modern PKE-to-KEM form with concrete bounds and correctness-error handling; this is the variant used by the NIST PQC KEMs (ML-KEM).

pages.class_justification: The transform is one fixed construction that calls the base scheme's algorithms and the hash functions only as oracles (derandomize with G, re-encrypt to check, derive the key with H); the IND-CCA reduction runs the adversary once as an oracle, simulating decapsulation from the adversary's random-oracle queries. Standard fully-black-box shape, within the ROM.
pages.model_justification: FO99 and HHK17 prove IND-CCA security only in the random-oracle model; a standard-model IND-CPA-to-IND-CCA lift is not known. The page already records model: rom — keep it, it is load-bearing.
pages.statement: The Fujisaki–Okamoto transform builds an [[key-encapsulation-mechanism#ind-cca-security|IND-CCA]]-secure [[key-encapsulation-mechanism|KEM]] in the [[random-oracle-model|random-oracle model]] from any [[key-encapsulation-mechanism#ind-cpa-kem|IND-CPA]]-secure (one-way-CPA suffices) base encryption scheme: encapsulation encrypts a random message $m$ under coins $G(m)$ and derives the session key as $H(m, c)$; decapsulation decrypts and re-encrypts to reject malformed ciphertexts [[FO99 - Secure Integration of Asymmetric and Symmetric Encryption Schemes|FO99]], [[HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation|HHK17]].
pages.sketch: Derandomizing encryption with $G(m)$ makes ciphertexts verifiable by re-encryption, so the reduction can answer decapsulation queries by searching the adversary's random-oracle queries for a message that re-encrypts to the submitted ciphertext; a CCA adversary that never queries the oracle on the challenge plaintext learns nothing about $H(m^*, c^*)$, and one that does yields a CPA (one-wayness) breaker.
pages.improvements_text: - Modular T/U decomposition with concrete bounds accounting for a $\delta$-correct base scheme; the implicit-rejection variant underlies the NIST PQC standard ML-KEM — [[HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation|HHK17]]
flags: HYPOTHESIS OBJECT MISMATCH: the standard FO statement (FO99, HHK17) takes an IND-CPA/OW-CPA *PKE* as the base scheme, not a KEM; ML-KEM applies FO to the K-PKE IND-CPA PKE. The claim as recorded (IND-CPA KEM ⇒ IND-CCA KEM in ROM) is still true — an IND-CPA KEM gives an IND-CPA PKE by hybrid, then FO applies — but the hypothesis should be re-pointed at IND-CPA PKE or the KEM→PKE step made explicit.

The source KEM page's claim that FO is 'used in all NIST PQC KEM standards (Kyber, NTRU)' is wrong: NTRU was a finalist, not a NIST standard (migration note confirmed; fix on key-encapsulation-mechanism.md, editor/skeptical-checker lane).
The KEM page's '[[learning-with-errors|Module LWE]]' wikilink conflates Module-LWE with plain LWE (migration note confirmed, other page).

sources.note: Defines semantic security and polynomial (indistinguishability) security and proves indistinguishability implies semantic security.

sources.ref_file_title: MRS88 - The Notion of Security for Probabilistic Cryptosystems
sources.authors: Silvio Micali, Charles Rackoff, Bob Sloan
sources.note: Proves the equivalence of semantic security, indistinguishability (GM), and Yao's definition, completing the equivalence. Extended abstract at CRYPTO 1986.

pages.class_justification: The construction in both directions is the identity map on schemes; each security reduction invokes the adversary of one notion once, as an oracle, to break the other notion. Fixed construction, fixed black-box reduction.
pages.statement: A [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] scheme is [[public-key-encryption#cpa-security|IND-CPA-secure]] if and only if it is semantically secure under chosen-plaintext attack: indistinguishability of encryptions and semantic security define the same class of schemes [[GM84 - Probabilistic encryption|GM84]], [[MRS88 - The Notion of Security for Probabilistic Cryptosystems|MRS88]].
pages.sketch: From indistinguishability, semantic security follows by simulation: the simulator runs the adversary on an encryption of a fixed message, and any advantage in computing $f(m)$ over the simulator yields a distinguisher between $\Enc(\pk, m)$ and the fixed-message ciphertext. Conversely, a distinguisher for a pair $(m_0, m_1)$ computes a plaintext predicate that no simulator without the ciphertext can predict beyond guessing.
flags: BROKEN TITLE/ANCHORS: the page is titled 'CPA Security ⇔ CPA Security' and both endpoints render as [[public-key-encryption#cpa-security]] because the variant ids ind-cpa-security and semantic-security both map to #cpa-security on the PKE page. The PKE page needs a distinct 'Semantic security' subsection/anchor, and this page should be retitled 'IND-CPA ⇔ semantic security'.

The migrated quote is from hybrid-argument and describes the many-query hybrid, which is a different (also standard) fact; the recorded edge is the notion equivalence, which is what the statement above sources.

pages.class_justification: The construction is the identity map on IBE schemes; the reduction runs the selective adversary unchanged as an adaptive adversary (it outputs the pre-committed challenge identity when asked). Fixed construction, fixed black-box reduction, advantage preserved exactly.
pages.statement: Every [[identity-based-encryption#ind-id-cpa-security|IND-ID-CPA-secure]] IBE scheme is [[identity-based-encryption#ind-sid-cpa-security-selective|IND-sID-CPA-secure]]: a selective adversary, which commits to its challenge identity $\mathit{id}^*$ before seeing $\pp$, is a special case of an adaptive adversary, so the identity map on schemes preserves the advantage exactly — folklore.
pages.sketch: Wrap the selective adversary as an adaptive one that submits the pre-committed $\mathit{id}^*$ as its adaptive challenge identity and forwards all extraction queries unchanged.
pages.security_loss: tight: the selective advantage equals the wrapped adaptive adversary's advantage
flags: The source page's phrase 'strictly weaker' also asserts a separation (selectively secure but not adaptively secure schemes exist); that separation is a distinct claim needing its own citation and is not covered by this edge.

sources.ref_file_title: BB04 - Efficient Selective-ID Secure Identity-Based Encryption Without Random Oracles
sources.note: Introduces the selective-ID model and the complexity-leveraging observation: an IBE with N identities that is (t, qS, eps)-selective-ID secure is (t, qS, N*eps)-fully secure. The explicit theorem appears in the Journal of Cryptology version (Efficient Selective Identity-Based Encryption Without Random Oracles, J. Cryptology 24(4), 2011, doi:10.1007/s00145-010-9078-6).

pages.class_justification: The construction is the identity map on IBE schemes; the reduction guesses the adaptive adversary's challenge identity uniformly, runs the adversary once as an oracle, and aborts on a wrong guess. Fixed construction, fixed black-box reduction.
pages.statement: Every [[identity-based-encryption#ind-sid-cpa-security-selective|IND-sID-CPA-secure]] IBE scheme with identity space $\calI$ is [[identity-based-encryption#ind-id-cpa-security|IND-ID-CPA-secure]] with a multiplicative security loss of $|\calI|$: the reduction guesses the challenge identity in advance and aborts on a wrong guess (complexity leveraging). For super-polynomial $|\calI|$ the loss is super-polynomial, so the implication requires sub-exponential selective security [[BB04 - Efficient Selective-ID Secure Identity-Based Encryption Without Random Oracles|BB04]].
pages.sketch: The reduction samples $\mathit{id}' \getsr \calI$, commits to it as its selective challenge, and runs the adaptive adversary; with probability $1/|\calI|$ the adversary's challenge identity equals $\mathit{id}'$, in which case the reduction forwards everything unchanged.
pages.security_loss: multiplicative factor $|\calI|$ (identity-space size); super-polynomial unless $|\calI| = \poly(\secpar)$, so super-polynomial identity spaces require sub-exponentially hard selective security
flags: SOURCE-PAGE ERROR CONFIRMED: identity-based-encryption.md line 97 says the leveraging argument 'incurs a polynomial security loss in $|\calI|$' — the loss is a factor of $|\calI|$ itself, which is exponential in the identity length; the IBE page prose should be fixed (skeptical-checker lane).

Verifier: confirm whether the explicit selective-to-adaptive theorem is in the EUROCRYPT 2004 / eprint 2004/172 version or only in the 2011 Journal of Cryptology version; if only the latter, the reference page may better carry the journal data (key BB04 either way — the literature cites the leveraging remark as [BB04]).

sources.ref_file_title: GPV08 - Trapdoors for hard lattices and new cryptographic constructions
sources.authors: Craig Gentry, Chris Peikert, Vinod Vaikuntanathan
sources.note: Full-domain-hash signatures from preimage-sampleable trapdoor functions; unforgeability from ISIS in the ROM.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction (hash-and-sign with a Gaussian preimage sampler); the unforgeability reduction runs any forger once as an oracle while programming the random oracle, and outputs an ISIS solution from the forgery. Black-box in both the assumption and the adversary, within the ROM.
pages.model_justification: GPV08 prove (strong) EUF-CMA security in the random-oracle model — the reduction programs $H$. The page currently says model: standard, which is wrong and must be corrected to rom (the migration notes already flag this).
pages.statement: [[shortest-integer-solution#isis-inhomogeneous-sis|ISIS]] hardness yields an EUF-CMA-secure (indeed strongly unforgeable) [[digital-signature|digital signature]] in the [[random-oracle-model|random-oracle model]]: the public key is $\mathbf{A} \in \ZZ_q^{n \times m}$, the secret key a lattice trapdoor for $\mathbf{A}$, and a signature on $\mu$ is a short $\mathbf{z}$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z} = H(\mu) \pmod q$, sampled with a discrete-Gaussian preimage sampler [[GPV08 - Trapdoors for hard lattices and new cryptographic constructions|GPV08]].
pages.sketch: The reduction answers oracle queries $H(\mu)$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}_\mu$ for self-sampled short Gaussian $\mathbf{z}_\mu$, so it signs without the trapdoor; a forgery on a fresh message is a short preimage of a uniform syndrome (an ISIS solution), and a forgery reusing a queried syndrome differs from the stored preimage with noticeable probability (preimage min-entropy), giving a short kernel vector.
notes_to_keep: The construction requires a trapdoor sampler for $\mathbf{A}$ (GPV08's preimage-sampleable functions); ISIS hardness gives unforgeability while the trapdoor enables signing — the source bullet on shortest-integer-solution.md elides this.
flags: MODEL FIX REQUIRED: frontmatter model: standard → rom. GPV signatures are only proven in the ROM.

pages.class_justification: Each direction is an oracle (Turing) reduction: it invokes a solver for the other problem as a black box on a rerandomized instance and post-processes the solution by linear algebra.
pages.statement: [[shortest-integer-solution#isis-inhomogeneous-sis|ISIS]] and [[shortest-integer-solution|SIS]] are polynomially equivalent under mild parameter conditions (sufficiently many columns, comparable norm bounds). One direction is immediate: splitting $\mathbf{A} = [\mathbf{A}' \mid \mathbf{a}]$ and obtaining from an ISIS oracle a short preimage of the uniform syndrome $\mathbf{a}$ under $\mathbf{A}'$ yields, after appending the coefficient $-1$, a nonzero short kernel vector of $\mathbf{A}$ — folklore.
pages.sketch: An ISIS oracle solves SIS with one call: for $\mathbf{A} = [\mathbf{A}' \mid \mathbf{a}]$ with $\mathbf{a}$ uniform, a short $\mathbf{z}'$ with $\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{a} \pmod q$ gives the SIS solution $(\mathbf{z}', -1)$, with norm bound $\sqrt{\beta^2 + 1}$.
notes_to_keep: The converse direction (using a SIS oracle to solve ISIS) is documented in the literature only as folklore — Ducas et al. (eprint 2023/1125) note it "seems folklore, though it has not been extensively documented beyond a comment by Peikert" — and its parameter conditions are load-bearing.
flags: Both problems independently enjoy the same worst-case hardness (Ajt96 for SIS; GPV08 prove worst-case hardness for ISIS directly), but that detour does not by itself give the average-case equivalence recorded here; the direct ISIS-to-SIS reduction is genuinely folklore and I could not find a paper proving it in full. Verifier may want to keep kind: equivalence but note the asymmetry in documentation.
The trailing GPV08 citation in the source sentence on shortest-integer-solution.md attaches to the signature construction, not the equivalence (migration note confirmed).

sources.ref_file_title: FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems
sources.note: Introduces the transform (challenges replaced by hashes of the transcript); stated for identification-to-signature, without proof. The ROM analysis for NIZK is later and often treated as standard.

sources.ref_file_title: FKMV12 - On the Non-malleability of the Fiat-Shamir Transform
sources.authors: Sebastian Faust, Markulf Kohlweiss, Giorgia Azzurra Marson, Daniele Venturi
sources.note: Formal ROM proofs that the transform gives zero knowledge, simulation soundness, and (weak) simulation extractability for Sigma protocols with quasi-unique responses.

pages.class_justification: One fixed compiler that runs the interactive protocol's prover and verifier as oracles, replacing challenges with hash values; the zero-knowledge simulator programs the random oracle, and the soundness reduction runs the cheating prover as an oracle, observing its RO queries. Black-box in both the protocol and the adversary, within the ROM.
pages.model_justification: The transform is proven only in the ROM; standard-model instantiation fails in general (GK03), as the page's own notes record.
pages.statement: Applying the Fiat–Shamir transform to a constant-round public-coin honest-verifier zero-knowledge [[interactive-protocol|interactive proof]] with negligible soundness error yields a [[non-interactive-zero-knowledge|NIZK]] argument in the [[random-oracle-model|random-oracle model]]: each verifier challenge is replaced by the hash of the statement and the transcript so far [[FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems|FS86]].
pages.sketch: The prover computes $c := H(x, a)$ in place of the verifier's challenge and outputs $(a, z)$; the zero-knowledge simulator samples an accepting transcript first and programs $H(x, a) := c$, and a cheating prover making $q$ oracle queries must answer a fresh uniform challenge for one of them, reducing to the interactive protocol's soundness with a factor-$q$ loss.
pages.improvements_text: - Zero knowledge, simulation soundness, and weak simulation extractability of the transform in the ROM, for $\Sigma$-protocols with quasi-unique responses — [[FKMV12 - On the Non-malleability of the Fiat-Shamir Transform|FKMV12]]
notes_to_keep: Soundness of the compiled protocol degrades with the number of rounds; beyond constant rounds the transform needs round-by-round (state-restoration) soundness of the underlying protocol.
The transform is known to fail in important settings when the oracle is instantiated with a concrete hash function (GK03, KRS25) — the model qualifier is load-bearing.
flags: HYPOTHESIS UNDERSPECIFIED (repairable): the edge quantifies over all interactive protocols, but the theorem needs public-coin, HVZK, negligible soundness error, and constant rounds; the statement above carries these qualifiers and they should reach the page.

NEAR-DUPLICATES: red-zkp-to-nizk-fs86, red-rom-and-zkp-to-nizk-fs86, and red-fiat-shamir-and-honest-verifier-zk-hvzk-to-nizk record essentially the same edge with different hypothesis slugs; consider consolidating.

pages.wrong_reason: Overbroad to the point of falsity: the Fiat–Shamir transform preserves the prover's communication, so an arbitrary interactive protocol plus the ROM cannot yield a *succinct* argument — succinctness must already reside in the hypothesis. Moreover FS applied to a multi-round or merely computationally sound protocol is not sound in general, even in the ROM (soundness degrades with rounds; the page's own notes cite the KRS25 attack on FS-GKR for the instantiated setting). The correct edges are: PCP + ROM ⇒ SNARG (Micali's CS proofs, Mic00: Silvio Micali, "Computationally Sound Proofs", SIAM J. Comput. 30(4), 2000) and public-coin IOP + ROM ⇒ SNARK (BCS16: Ben-Sasson, Chiesa, Spooner, "Interactive Oracle Proofs", TCC 2016). A separate page, red-ip-and-rom-to-snark-fs86, already records the same overbroad claim with hypotheses {ip, rom}; both should be replaced by edges whose hypothesis is the PCP/IOP object.
flags: DUPLICATE: same claim as red-ip-and-rom-to-snark-fs86 (not in this batch), which cites FS86 and has the same overbreadth problem; the two pages should be consolidated into correctly-hypothesized edges (PCP + ROM ⇒ SNARG, Mic00; public-coin IOP + ROM ⇒ SNARK, BCS16). Neither Mic00 nor BCS16 has a reference page yet.

pages.class_justification: The construction is the identity map that forgets $\Invert$; the reduction runs any PRF distinguisher unchanged as an iPRF distinguisher that never queries its inversion oracle. Fixed construction, fixed black-box reduction, advantage preserved exactly.
pages.statement: An [[pseudorandom-function#invertible-prfs|invertible PRF]] $(\KeyGen, \Eval, \Invert)$ is a [[pseudorandom-function|PRF]] with an added inversion algorithm: discarding $\Invert$ leaves a PRF, and any PRF distinguisher is an iPRF distinguisher that ignores its inversion oracle, so the advantage is preserved exactly — folklore.
pages.sketch: Immediate restriction: the iPRF security game with the inversion oracles removed is exactly $\Game^{\mathrm{prf}}$, so a PRF distinguisher against $(\KeyGen, \Eval)$ breaks the iPRF's (strong or plain) pseudorandomness without ever using $\Invert$.
pages.security_loss: tight: the PRF advantage equals the iPRF advantage of the wrapped distinguisher
notes_to_keep: Definitional 'extends' relation (an iPRF is a PRF plus $\Invert$); 'invertible-prf'/'iPRF' is an anchor of the PRF page itself rather than a distinct object, so the edge is self-referential in the current slug scheme.
flags: The iPRF notion as defined on the PRF page follows HPPY25 (Plinko), which the wiki already cites for the converse edge prf-to-invertible-prf-hppy25; this forward edge is purely definitional and could arguably live as a sentence on the PRF page rather than as a reduction page.

pages.wrong_reason: False as recorded at base-class granularity: the wiki's interactive-proof-systems page defines IP with polynomially many rounds (IP = PSPACE), and its arthur-merlin page defines AM as the two-message class (with AM[k] = AM for constant k). 'IP ⊆ AM' therefore asserts PSPACE ⊆ AM, which is not known and widely disbelieved (AM ⊆ Π₂ᵖ, so it would collapse PH). GS86 proves the round-preserving statement IP[k] ⊆ AM[k+2] for every k — the quote the page migrated says exactly this. The correct base-class corollaries are: constant-round IP ⊆ AM, and IP[poly] = AM[poly] (= PSPACE). The edge needs round-indexed objects or a hypothesis restricted to constant-round IP; as recorded it should not stand, especially with status: draft and class: free.
flags: HIGH PRIORITY: the false inclusion is live on the site (status: draft, class: free) and appears in the generated 'Participates in' sections of both interactive-proof-systems.md and arthur-merlin.md. The sibling GS86 edges bpp-to-am-gs86 / np-to-am-gs86 / conp-to-am-gs86 are fine; only this one loses the round parameter fatally.
